title: Lesson 6: Communicating Concerns to the Right Person
summary: Report concerns through the right channel rather than letting problems grow through silence, assumptions, gossip or unproductive complaints.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Reporting, escalation, professional communication, accountability and problem-solving

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a therapist discovers that the air conditioner in a treatment room is not working properly.
Instead of informing the supervisor or the person responsible for maintenance, she complains to several colleagues.
Throughout the day, employees discuss how uncomfortable the room has become.
However, nobody reports the problem to someone who can arrange a repair.
Eventually, a client arrives for a massage session and complains about the temperature.
Management only becomes aware of the problem after the client's experience has already been affected.
Now imagine a different response.

The therapist notices the problem and promptly informs the appropriate supervisor: "The air conditioner in Room 2 is not cooling properly. I've noticed the room becoming uncomfortable. Could you please advise whether we should use another room while the issue is addressed?"
The supervisor can now assess the situation, arrange appropriate action and communicate any necessary changes.

The difference is not simply that one employee noticed a problem. Both employees noticed it. The difference is that one complained to people who could not resolve it, while the other communicated the concern to someone who could take action.
At Zura Spa, employees must learn to report concerns through appropriate channels rather than allowing problems to grow through silence, assumptions, gossip or unnecessary complaints.

sections.title: 2. What does communicating concerns to the right person mean?
paragraphs: It means identifying a problem, understanding who has the responsibility or authority to address it and communicating the relevant information clearly and promptly.
Effective reporting is not about finding someone to blame. It is about ensuring that the right person receives the information needed to address the issue.
list: Client satisfaction or complaints.
Workplace safety.
Treatment-room preparation.
Equipment or supply problems.
Employee behaviour.
Scheduling difficulties.
Misunderstandings between colleagues.
Workload and operational challenges.
Confidentiality or privacy.
Suspected misconduct.
Unclear instructions.
Personal difficulties affecting work performance.

sections.title: 1. Problems can be resolved earlier
paragraphs: Timely reporting gives the responsible person an opportunity to act before the issue becomes more serious.

sections.title: 2. Client safety and satisfaction are protected
paragraphs: Concerns affecting treatment, hygiene, comfort or service quality can be addressed appropriately.

sections.title: 3. Teamwork improves
paragraphs: Employees spend less time blaming one another and more time finding solutions.

sections.title: 4. Misunderstandings are reduced
paragraphs: Clear communication helps management and supervisors understand what actually happened.

sections.title: 5. Accountability is strengthened
paragraphs: Employees take responsibility for raising concerns instead of silently allowing avoidable problems to continue.

sections.title: 6. Workplace trust increases
paragraphs: A culture of responsible reporting helps employees feel that concerns can be raised and addressed fairly.

sections.title: 4. The difference between complaining and reporting
paragraphs: Complaining and reporting are not always the same.
An employee may express frustration because something is genuinely wrong. However, if the concern is never communicated to someone who can address it, the problem may remain unresolved.
Employees should not be discouraged from expressing genuine dissatisfaction. The goal is to help concerns reach the appropriate person and receive proper attention.
table: Repeatedly discussing a problem without seeking action
Focusing mainly on blame or insults
Discussing sensitive matters with uninvolved employees
Confirming that the concern has been received
Expecting others to guess what is wrong
Explaining the support or action needed

sections.title: Example — complaining versus reporting
paragraphs: Unproductive complaint: "Nothing ever works properly in this place. Everybody is just careless."
Constructive report: "The water supply in Room 3 is not functioning properly. I noticed the issue while preparing for the next appointment. Please, who should I inform so it can be addressed?"
The second statement identifies the problem and moves toward a solution.

sections.title: 5. Identifying the right person to contact
paragraphs: Not every concern should be directed to the same person.
The appropriate contact depends on the nature, seriousness and urgency of the issue, as well as Zura Spa's established reporting structure.
This table illustrates typical reporting routes; employees should follow the reporting arrangements formally communicated by Zura Spa.
table: Reception or the staff member responsible for scheduling
Assigned supervisor or person responsible for supplies
Responsible staff member or supervisor, depending on seriousness and authority
Immediate supervisor or person coordinating the shift
Respectful direct discussion where appropriate, or supervisor support
Appropriate senior management or designated reporting channel
Immediate danger or serious safety risk
Take necessary immediate safety action and contact the appropriate emergency or responsible personnel

sections.title: An important exception
paragraphs: If the person normally responsible for receiving a report is involved in the misconduct, has a conflict of interest or is failing to address a serious concern, employees should be able to use an appropriate alternative or higher-level reporting channel.
Reporting concerns to the right person does not mean employees must remain silent when their immediate supervisor is part of the problem.

sections.title: 6. Seven principles of communicating concerns professionally
Principle 1: Report concerns promptly
paragraphs: Do not unnecessarily delay reporting problems that may affect clients, employees or operations.
A small issue can become more difficult to resolve when it is ignored.
Example: A therapist notices that an essential supply is almost finished. She should communicate the shortage before it disrupts an appointment.

sections.title: Principle 2: Communicate facts rather than assumptions
paragraphs: Explain what you observed without presenting unverified conclusions as facts.
Instead of: "The receptionist deliberately refused to prepare the booking."
Say: "The booking had not been confirmed when I checked. I would like to understand what happened."

sections.title: Principle 3: Be clear and specific
paragraphs: A useful report should explain what happened, where it happened and why attention is needed.
Vague: "There is a problem with the room."
Clear: "The air conditioner in Room 2 is not cooling properly, and the room is becoming uncomfortable."

sections.title: Principle 4: Choose an appropriate communication channel
paragraphs: Some concerns can be communicated through routine workplace messages.
Others require a private conversation, urgent phone call or formal report.
Sensitive employee matters should not be discussed in general staff groups.

sections.title: Principle 5: Focus on resolution
paragraphs: Where possible, explain what assistance or decision is needed.
Example: "The room is not ready because clean towels are unavailable. Could we arrange additional towels or use another prepared room?"

sections.title: Principle 6: Maintain confidentiality
paragraphs: Share sensitive information only with people who have a legitimate reason to receive it.
Avoid turning a workplace concern into gossip.

sections.title: Principle 7: Follow up appropriately
paragraphs: If the concern remains unresolved, follow up through the appropriate channel.
Serious or urgent concerns may require escalation rather than waiting indefinitely.

sections.title: 7. How to communicate a concern clearly
paragraphs: A useful workplace report should answer five basic questions.
list: What happened? Describe the issue accurately.
Where and when did it happen? Provide relevant location and timing.
What is the impact or potential risk? Explain how the issue affects clients, staff or operations.
What action has already been taken? Mention any steps completed or temporary measures used.
What assistance or decision is needed? State the next action you are requesting, if known.

sections.title: Example — a clear report
paragraphs: "Good afternoon. The air conditioner in Room 2 stopped cooling properly at approximately 2 p.m. The room is becoming uncomfortable, and we have a client scheduled for 3 p.m. I have checked that the unit is switched on, but the problem remains. Please, can we arrange an alternative room while the issue is addressed?"
This report is clear, factual and solution-focused.

sections.title: 8. Reporting concerns about colleagues
paragraphs: Concerns about coworkers should be handled carefully.
Employees should avoid turning misunderstandings into accusations or discussing private matters with uninvolved staff.
Lesson: Professional reporting should protect fairness and dignity while allowing genuine concerns to be addressed.

sections.title: When direct communication may be appropriate
paragraphs: If the issue is minor, safe to address directly and does not involve serious misconduct, a respectful conversation may help.
Example: "I noticed the supplies were not replenished after the last session. Can we agree on how to make sure they are ready for the next appointment?"

sections.title: When supervisor involvement may be appropriate
list: The issue continues despite reasonable attempts to resolve it.
Work responsibilities are being affected.
Employees cannot reach an appropriate agreement.
The concern involves repeated unprofessional behaviour.
A decision or intervention is needed.

sections.title: When direct confrontation is not appropriate
paragraphs: Employees should not be expected to confront someone directly when the concern involves threats, harassment, coercion, serious misconduct or a reasonable fear of retaliation.
In such cases, use an appropriate reporting channel.

sections.title: 9. Reporting client complaints
paragraphs: Client complaints should be taken seriously.
Employees should listen carefully, avoid unnecessary defensiveness and communicate the issue to someone authorised to address it.
The employee should report the facts without making unsupported judgments about the therapist.

sections.title: Appropriate steps
list: Listen to the client's concern.
Acknowledge the concern respectfully.
Clarify the relevant details.
Explain what you can appropriately do.
Refer the matter to the responsible person when necessary.
Provide accurate updates without promising unauthorised outcomes.

sections.title: Example — a client complaint about pressure
paragraphs: A client complains that the massage pressure was not adjusted after she requested a lighter touch.
Inappropriate response: "That therapist always has complaints."
Professional response: "Thank you for telling us. I'm sorry your preference was not followed. I will bring this to the appropriate supervisor's attention so the concern can be reviewed."

sections.title: 10. Reporting mistakes and incidents
paragraphs: Employees may sometimes make mistakes.
A professional employee should not conceal an error simply because she fears embarrassment or correction.
Reporting a mistake is not the same as being careless. Concealing a known mistake can create a much more serious problem.

sections.title: Example — a wrong appointment time
paragraphs: A receptionist accidentally records the wrong appointment time.
She notices the mistake before the client arrives.
Inappropriate response: Ignore the error and hope it does not cause a problem.

Professional response: "I noticed that I entered the wrong appointment time. I've identified the correct details and would like to confirm the appropriate steps to correct the booking and inform the client."

sections.title: Why prompt reporting matters
list: It allows mistakes to be corrected earlier.
It reduces unnecessary disruption.
It protects clients and colleagues.
It supports accountability.
It helps the organisation identify improvements.

sections.title: 11. Escalation: Knowing when to involve a higher authority
paragraphs: Escalation means referring a concern to someone with greater responsibility, authority or specialised ability to address it.
Not every concern requires immediate escalation to senior management.
However, some concerns should not remain at the level of routine workplace discussion.
Employees should not delay emergency assistance or urgent protective action while following ordinary reporting steps.

sections.title: Examples of concerns requiring prompt escalation
list: Serious client safety concerns.
Harassment, threats or abusive behaviour.
Suspected theft or fraud.
Serious confidentiality breaches.
Repeated misconduct.
A supervisor's involvement in alleged wrongdoing.
Unresolved issues that create significant operational or safety risks.
Concerns that the responsible person has failed to address appropriately.

sections.title: Appropriate escalation process
list: Identify the concern and its seriousness.
Take any necessary immediate safety action.
Report to the appropriate responsible person or designated channel.
Provide accurate facts and relevant evidence.
Request clarification on the next steps where appropriate.
Escalate further if the concern remains serious, unresolved or improperly handled.

sections.title: 12. A practical method: The REPORT approach

items.label: R — Recognise the concern
items.body: Identify what is wrong and why it requires attention.

items.label: O — Outline the issue clearly
items.body: Explain what happened, the impact and any action already taken.

items.label: R — Request appropriate action
items.body: Communicate the assistance or decision needed.

items.label: T — Track and follow up
items.body: Confirm that the concern has reached the responsible person and follow up according to its urgency.

sections.title: 13. Common reporting mistakes to avoid
table: Inform the person responsible for resolving the issue
State what you personally know and what remains unverified
Waiting until a small problem becomes serious
Blaming someone without understanding the situation
Describe the issue and seek clarification
Explain what, where, when, impact and action needed
Assuming someone else has reported the issue
Confirm that the concern has reached the appropriate person
Use the appropriate reporting or escalation channel

sections.title: Case study A: The broken equipment
paragraphs: A therapist notices that a piece of equipment is not functioning correctly.
She tells two colleagues but does not inform the supervisor.
The equipment is used again, and the problem becomes worse.
Expected lesson: Equipment problems should be reported promptly to the responsible person, with appropriate safety precautions.
list: What did the therapist do incorrectly?
Who should have received the report?
Why was discussing the issue with colleagues insufficient?
What immediate precautions may have been appropriate?
How should the concern have been communicated?

sections.title: Case study B: The unhappy employee
paragraphs: An employee believes her workload is unfair.
Instead of speaking with the supervisor, she repeatedly complains to colleagues.
The complaints create tension, but the workload issue remains unresolved.
Expected lesson: Genuine workplace concerns are more likely to be addressed when communicated constructively through appropriate channels.
list: Is the employee's concern potentially legitimate?
Why has the current approach not resolved it?
How should she communicate the concern?
What information would help the supervisor assess the issue?

sections.title: Case study C: The client complaint
paragraphs: A client tells a therapist that she is dissatisfied with part of her service.
The therapist becomes defensive and does not inform anyone.
Later, the client contacts management directly.
Expected lesson: Client complaints should be acknowledged and referred appropriately rather than concealed or dismissed.
list: What should the therapist have done?
Why is it important to report client complaints?
How could the concern have been handled professionally?
What should the therapist avoid saying?

sections.title: Case study D: The serious misconduct concern
paragraphs: An employee observes behaviour that may violate professional standards.
The person involved is a senior colleague who tells her not to report the incident.
Expected lesson: Serious concerns must be reportable through appropriate channels, including alternatives when the usual reporting person is involved.
list: Should the employee remain silent?
What reporting options should be available?
Why might direct confrontation be inappropriate?
How should the organisation protect the integrity of the reporting process?

sections.title: 15. Practical group activity: Who should receive the report?
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees identify appropriate reporting routes and practise clear communication.
Expected outcome: Participants should recognise that different concerns require different reporting routes and levels of urgency.

sections.title: Instructions
paragraphs: Divide participants into small groups. Present the following situations.
list: A treatment room has run out of clean towels.
A client requests a change to an appointment.
A colleague repeatedly fails to complete an assigned task.
A client reports an uncomfortable massage experience.
An employee suspects that private client information has been shared improperly.
An employee experiences threatening or harassing conduct from a supervisor.

sections.title: For each situation, identify
list: Who should receive the concern?
How urgent is the issue?
What facts should be communicated?
What immediate action may be needed?
When should the matter be escalated?

sections.title: 16. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 6 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the main purpose of communicating concerns to the right person? To make sure everyone hears about the problem / To ensure the concern reaches someone who can appropriately address it / To avoid taking responsibility
You notice a treatment-room equipment problem. What should you do? Report it promptly and follow appropriate safety procedures / Discuss it only with friends / Ignore it until a client complains

A colleague tells you about suspected serious misconduct involving a supervisor. What is appropriate? Share the story in the general staff group / Remain silent because the supervisor is senior / Use an appropriate alternative or higher-level reporting channel

Which statement is the most constructive workplace report? Everybody here is careless. / Room 2's air conditioner is not cooling, and a client is scheduled soon. Could we arrange an alternative? / Nothing ever works.
What should you do if a serious concern remains unresolved? Follow up and escalate through an appropriate channel / Assume it no longer matters / Spread the issue to uninvolved colleagues

sections.title: 17. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what communicating concerns to the right person means.
Identify five types of workplace concerns that should be reported.
Explain the difference between unproductive complaining and constructive reporting.
Describe how you would report a treatment-room equipment problem.
Explain why employees should communicate mistakes promptly.
What should an employee do if a serious concern involves the person they would normally report to?
Describe the REPORT method in your own words.
Explain why confidentiality matters when reporting concerns.
Identify three personal habits you intend to improve when communicating workplace concerns.

sections.title: 18. Seven-day reporting challenge
table: Identify the correct reporting person for common workplace issues
Practise describing a concern using facts rather than assumptions
Report a genuine operational issue promptly if one arises
Avoid discussing sensitive concerns with uninvolved colleagues
Practise communicating a problem together with the assistance needed
Review appropriate escalation routes for serious concerns
Reflect on how responsible reporting supports teamwork

sections.title: 19. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Problems are a normal part of workplace operations.
What matters is how employees respond when those problems arise.
At Zura Spa, employees should not allow concerns to remain unresolved because of silence, fear, gossip or unnecessary complaints.
They should communicate clearly, provide accurate information and direct concerns to the people responsible for addressing them.
Management and supervisors must also create an environment where employees can raise genuine concerns without unnecessary intimidation or retaliation.
Next topic: Professional Communication on Workplace WhatsApp Groups.

remember: A problem discussed with the wrong people may remain a problem. A concern communicated to the right person creates an opportunity for action. At Zura Spa, professionalism means speaking up responsibly, reporting facts accurately, protecting confidentiality and helping the team find solutions. Do not merely complain about what is wrong—communicate it appropriately so something can be done.
